1: Y'all, I ain't gon' hold you, when Gout Gout ran nineteen sixty-seven back in April, I said it was fake. And dat lil comment went everywhere. Yahoo, SportBible, Runner's Tribe, dey all quoted me, and a whole bunch of y'all called me a hater. So I went back and pulled every race he ran, every time, every wind readin', every dude in dem races. And by da time I'm done, y'all gon' see exactly why I said what I said.
2: Gout Gout was born December twenty-ninth, two thousand seven, in Ipswich, Queensland, out dere in Australia. His mama and daddy came from South Sudan. He was out dere playin' soccer when his coach, Di Sheppard, seen him. And her story crazy. She ain't have no track background at all. Back in da early two thousands she was workin' at a grocery store, and her son was a fast lil kid at Ipswich Grammar. Dey told her only people who work at da school can coach, so she quit da grocery store and took a job handin' out school uniforms, just so she could coach. Years later she see dis tall skinny kid runnin' 'round wit' his homies, and she said, who dat? I want him. And she been his only coach ever since.
3: Then in December twenty twenty-four, at sixteen, he ran twenty oh four in da two hundred at da All Schools meet. Dat broke Peter Norman Australian record from da nineteen sixty-eight Olympics. Fifty-six years, y'all. And it was faster than Usain Bolt ran at sixteen. A couple months before dat, adidas signed him, and folks online started throwin' numbers 'round. Four million. Six million. Ain't nobody ever confirmed a number. Not adidas, not his manager, nobody. But just like dat, everybody started callin' him da next Usain Bolt.
4: But here go da first thing I noticed. Before twenty twenty-six, every time dis dude went under ten seconds or under twenty seconds, it was wind-aided. Ten oh four wit' a three point four tailwind. Nineteen ninety-eight wit' a three point four. Nine ninety-nine, twice, in one day, wit' a three point five and a two point six. Nineteen eighty-four wit' a two point two. Da legal limit is two point oh. And every last one of dem was ran at home, down dere in Australia.
5: Yeah, in twenty twenty-five he went overseas and ran twenty oh two in da Czech Republic wit' zero wind. Dat's da one legal time everybody gon' throw at me. But put him in a real championship, da World Championships in Tokyo, and he run twenty twenty-three in his heat, twenty thirty-six in da semi, and he ain't even make da final.
6: Then come twenty twenty-six. His first race of da year, February twenty-first in Brisbane, he run ten flat in da hundred. Wind plus point nine. Legal. But look at da rest of dat meet. Six of da wind readin's dat day was over da limit, and one of da men's hundreds was a plus two point eight. Then da rest of da season? Ten twenty. Ten nineteen. Ten forty-four. Ten twenty-one. He ain't never came close to dat ten flat again.
7: And da two hundred was da same story. At da Queensland champs he ran twenty fifty-nine and twenty forty-two, and he said he was sick. Then at da Maurie Plant meet in Melbourne, in da rain, Lachlan Kennedy went and beat him, twenty thirty-eight to twenty forty-three. 8: Now here go da race. April twelfth, Sydney, da national championships. In da mornin' heat he run twenty eleven. Dat afternoon in da final, nineteen sixty-seven, and da wind gauge say plus one point seven. Now listen. Da women's two hundred final, right before dem, read plus two point three. Illegal. Same track, same afternoon, minutes apart. And look at da men's final. Seven of da eight dudes ran a personal best, and every single one of 'em ran way faster than dey did in da heat dat mornin'. Aidan Murphy came in wit' a twenty forty-one best and ran nineteen eighty-eight. Yeah, World Athletics ratified it, I know. Da gauge said legal. But I'm tellin' y'all, dat race was windy. Ain't no way a whole final PR da same day by accident.
9: Now let's go down da line. Every dude in dat final, and what he ran his very next two hundred. Gout, nineteen sixty-seven. His next two hundred, Oslo, twenty sixty. Almost a full second slower. Aidan Murphy, nineteen eighty-eight. Next race, da Oceania champs, twenty twenty-eight in da heat, twenty oh five in da final. Calab Law, twenty twenty-one. Next race, Tokyo, twenty eighty-five. Christopher Ius, twenty twenty-six. Next race, twenty-one oh two in da heat, twenty sixty-eight in da final. Archer McHugh, twenty thirty-seven. He ain't run another two hundred da rest of da year. 10: Now here go where it get crazy. Two months later in Oslo, his Diamond League debut, he ran twenty sixty and finished sixth. Then he ran a hundred fifty in Ostrava and got third. So June twenty-ninth, I went on TikTok and I said dis.
10b: Then July fourth, at da Pre Classic in Eugene, Tate Taylor ran nineteen seventy-five, into a minus point nine headwind. Gout was supposed to be in dat race. He pulled out, sayin' tightness. 11: So here go my verdict. Take away dat one day in Sydney, and Gout Gout ain't never broke twenty legal. Not one time. His next best legal time is twenty oh two. All year long in twenty twenty-six, outside of Sydney, he was runnin' twenty point four, twenty point five, twenty point six. Meanwhile Tate Taylor ran nineteen seventy-five into a headwind.
